newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Ross brings Israeli officials to Arafat - PLO.
newsitem.headline: Ross brings Israeli officials to Arafat - PLO.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross brought Israeli government officials together with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Sunday, the first such meeting since Islamic militant suicide bombers threw peace moves into deeper crisis.
A Palestine Liberation Organisation official told Reuters Ross took Israeli negotiator Yitzhak Molho and Shin Bet secret police chief Ami Ayalon with him to a meeting with Arafat in Ramallah.
He said a third Israeli was with the group but he did not have that man's name.
"The meeting is focusing on security and political issues but mainly on security issues," the PLO official, who spoke on condition he not be named, said.

"We want the Israelis to give us more information on their investigations on the attack and we are going to inform them of the measures we have taken so far in battling terrorism. We have uncovered a lot of things that we will tell them about."
Ross's delegation travelled to Ramallah from Jerusalem where had just ended his second meeting of the day with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Ross had walked into a Middle East war of words when he arrived on a mission to revive Israeli-Palestinian peace moves blown off course by the suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market 10 days ago.
"I have a sense that there's a desire to find ways to move forward but it will take a lot of work," Ross had told Israel's Channel Two television.

Netanyahu told the U.S. Cable News Network: "This is the message that I give, and I hope he (Ross) gives, to Yasser Arafat: 'Fight terrorism for the sake of peace. If you don't fight terrorism, peace will be endangered'."
"He (Ross) made it patently clear that he would not engage the Palestinians on political matters until they assured him and assured us that they would fight terrorism," Netanyahu said.
But Arafat pointedly told reporters after his first meeting with the U.S. envoy in the West Bank self-ruled town of Ramallah that "talks were not confined to security matters".

Palestinian officials said they were discussing with Ross a U.S. initiative which Secretary of State Madeleine Albright could bring with her on a possible maiden trip to the Middle East at the end of the month.
President Bill Clinton and Albright sent Ross to ease tensions heightened by a July 30 attack which killed 15 people including the two Islamic militant bombers.
"The president and the secretary want me to focus on the security questions and I will be doing that," Ross told reporters after his first meeting with Netanyahu in Jerusalem.
He said Clinton and Albright recognised there was "a political dimension that has to be addressed but they also understand that there is an essential security underpinning to the (peace) process".

Arafat wants Israel to stop construction of a Jewish settlement it calls Har Homa in Arab East Jerusalem, an end to Palestinian house demolitions and land confiscations, and the lifting of a closure imposed on Palestinians over the attack.

"We especially discussed the Israeli measures against the Palestinian people," Arafat said of his meeting with Ross. He said Palestinians were demanding that any further Israeli-PLO security contacts be witnessed by U.S. officials.
The Israeli army lifted an "inner closure" in parts of the West Bank on Sunday, allowing Palestinians to travel between three besieged self-ruled cities -- Jenin, Tulkarm and Qalqilya.
It opened crossings linking the West Bank and Gaza with Jordan and Egypt for travel by Palestinians and others.

Israeli soldiers would continue to surround the West Bank cities of Hebron, Ramallah and Bethlehem and an overall ban on Palestinians entering Israel remained in effect, the army said. A siege of Jericho and Nablus was lifted on Friday.

But as bulldozers continued digging on Har Homa on Sunday, Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan said: "There's no chance we will stop the construction on Har Homa...There is no connection between the construction in Har Homa and the settlements...and the terrorism."
Ross said Albright was prepared to visit at the end of the month provided progress was made on security.
Her trip would likely be aimed at finding ways to wrap up outstanding issues from interim Israel-PLO deals and pursue accelerated talks on a final peace settlement.
In a television interview on Saturday, Arafat said he was making a "100 percent effort" to arrest militants.
